hook.text: A single large cargo ship can emit as much SO₂ as 50 million cars.

buildup.text: Ships burn the dirtiest fuel on Earth — heavy fuel oil, thick as tar and full of sulfur.

discovery.text: New rules since 2020 cap sulfur in ship fuel at 0.5%, down from 3.5%.

twist.text: Aviation trails create thin clouds that trap heat — adding warming beyond just the CO₂.

climax.text: International shipping and flying combined produce about 5% of global CO₂ emissions.

punchline.text: Global trade floats on some of the dirtiest fuel ever burned.

quiz.question: What type of fuel do large cargo ships traditionally burn?

details.summary: International shipping and aviation together produce significant sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and particulate emissions largely beyond national regulatory reach. A single large container ship can emit as much SOx as millions of cars.
details.whyItMatters: As global trade and travel grow, shipping and aviation pollution rises. These sectors face unique regulatory challenges because they operate across borders.
takeaways: Ships burning heavy fuel oil emit massive amounts of SO2
Aviation NOx at altitude contributes to ozone formation
The IMO 2020 sulfur cap cut ship fuel sulfur limits by 86 percent

faq.question: Why do ships produce so much sulfur dioxide?
faq.answer: Ships traditionally burn heavy fuel oil, a thick residual fuel with sulfur content up to 3.5 percent. The IMO 2020 regulation capped sulfur at 0.5 percent, but enforcement on the open ocean remains challenging.

faq.question: How does aviation affect air quality at high altitude?
faq.answer: Aircraft engines emit NOx at cruising altitude where it catalyzes ozone formation in the upper troposphere. Contrails and cirrus clouds from exhaust also trap heat, adding a warming effect beyond CO2 alone.
